### Observed differences

- In the earlier window, each of A28, A29, A31, A32, A33, A34, A35 and A36 appeared exactly once in every one of the 200 cases (participation 100%). In the later window, each of these eight activities appears in only about 50 in 100 cases (100–101 of 200), still once per case when present, while A25 and A26 continue to appear in every case in both windows. [OCC001, OCC002, OCC003, OCC004, OCC005, OCC006, OCC007, OCC008, POS001, POS002]
- Before, an activity from the group A28/A29/A31/A32 and one from the group A33/A34/A35/A36 always occurred in the same case, with the first group always before the second (200 of 200 cases). In the later window, such cross-group pairs share a case in only about 1 in 200 cases; in roughly half the cases only the first-group activity appears, and in roughly half only the second-group one. [REL020, REL023, REL026, REL029, REL031, REL035, REL038]
- A25 still precedes whichever group runs and A26 still follows it in both windows; earlier the sequence A25 → first group → second group → A26 held in every case, and the order within each group stayed roughly balanced (about 50/50 for within-group pairs) in both windows. [REL001, REL005, REL009, REL013, REL017, REL030, REL039, REL044]
- Before, the outgoing transitions of A25 went only to first-group activities (A31 about 30%, A29 about 27%, A32 about 26%, A28 about 18%); in the later window they spread over all eight group activities (roughly 10–15% each), and first-group activities now lead directly to A26 in about a quarter of their transitions (for example A28→A26 about 25%, A32→A26 about 29%) instead of flowing on into the second group. [DIR001, DIR002, DIR003, DIR004, DIR005]
- Measured event distances changed accordingly: the gap from A25 to second-group activities, previously always at the largest measured lag (5) whenever the pair fell within the five-step window, now spreads over lags 1–4; the gap from first-group activities to A26 similarly spread from only lag 5 to lags 1–4; cross-group pairs fall within five steps in only about one later-window observation. [LAG001, LAG002, LAG003, LAG004, LAG005, LAG008, LAG013, LAG017, LAG006, LAG014]
- Mean relative positions shifted (A25 about 0.58→0.66 of the trace, first-group activities about 0.65→0.74, second-group activities about 0.77→0.73–0.75, A26 0.84→0.82), consistent with traces containing one group instead of two, though a position shift alone does not show that an activity was moved. [POS001, POS002, POS003, POS004, POS005, POS006, POS007, POS008, POS009, POS010]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The screening flagged 90 evidence items where fewer than one (about 0.84) would be expected for an unchanged process, and each difference exceeds about 995 of 1000 random re-splits of the pooled data, so the overall volume cannot be explained by chance; the items largely describe one underlying difference rather than independent changes. The evidence supports the hypothesis that the two four-activity groups became mutually exclusive alternatives: in the later window a case executes either A28, A29, A31 and A32 or A33, A34, A35 and A36 between A25 and A26, in roughly a 50/50 split, whereas earlier every case executed both groups in sequence (first group, then second group). This is shown directly by relational evidence — cross-group co-occurrence fell from all cases to about 1 in 200, with one-sided appearances splitting about 50/50 — and is consistent across participation, routing and distance indicators. [REL020, REL031, OCC001, DIR001, LAG001]

Limitations: the split is symmetric, so the evidence cannot establish which group was newly made optional versus required, and one later-window case still contains both groups, so exclusivity may not be absolute. A competing explanation the evidence cannot rule out is a changed mix of case types between the windows rather than a routing change within one process. The roughly 50/50 shares are sample estimates, although sampling differences in variant frequencies cannot plausibly explain the overall difference, since a variant present in half the cases would not be missed by the 200-case earlier window. [REL020]

Let me analyze this evidence carefully.

90 items vs 0.84 expected without change — that's more than 100x the expectation. So the count is many times larger than chance; this cannot be explained by chance as a whole. So we move past the "insufficient evidence by count" gate.

Now, what's the underlying behaviour? Let me piece it together.

OCC items: A28, A29, A31, A32, A33, A34, A35, A36 all decreased from participation 1.0 to ~0.5, mean occurrences per trace from 1.0 to ~0.5. So in the before window, every trace contained each of these activities exactly once; in the after window, only about half the traces contain each of them (once).

REL items: pairs among {A25, A26} × {A28, A29, A31, A32, A33, A34, A35, A36}:

- REL009-016: (A26, B): before co-occurrence 1.0, B_before_A = 1.0 (i.e., B before A26). After: co-occurrence 0.5, A_only 0.5 (A26 only), B_before_A 0.5.
- REL017-019, 024, 025, 030: pairs among {A28, A29, A31, A32}: before co-occurrence 1.0 with roughly 50/50 order; after co-occurrence 0.5, neither 0.5 (i.e., in half the traces neither appears — consistent with the half of traces where these activities are skipped), and in the co-occurring half the order is ~50/50.
